theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

options: It can catch fire from sparks or spatter

essays.stem: You are the team leader for a fabrication bay used by five welders. Explain how you would plan the housekeeping for the bay over a working week.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would list the housekeeping tasks for the bay: removing slag, stubs and offcuts, cleaning up dust, emptying scrap and waste bins, checking cables and hoses, cleaning the booths, benches and extraction hoods, and checking that exits and extinguishers are clear. Then I would decide how often each task is done: some as the work goes, some at the end of each shift, and some weekly, such as cleaning the extractor filters as the maker's manual says. I would write a roster that gives each task to a named person, so the work is shared fairly, and allow time for it in the job plan. I would make sure the right brooms, vacuum, bins, spill kit and PPE are there. At a toolbox talk I would explain the roster and the reasons for it. Each day I would check that the tasks are done, and at the end of the week I would inspect the bay with a checklist, record the score and agree actions for any faults.
markingPoints: Lists the housekeeping tasks for the bay
Sets how often each task is done (as you go, each shift, weekly, filters as the maker says)
Roster with a named person for each task, and time allowed in the job plan
Makes sure cleaning equipment, bins, spill kit and PPE are available
Explains the plan to the team, checks daily and inspects and records weekly

essays.stem: Describe the five steps of the 5S method and give a fabrication workshop example of each step.
essays.modelAnswer: 5S is a method for keeping a workplace organised, safe and efficient. Sort: go through the area and remove anything not needed for the work, such as broken tools, old offcuts and empty tins; red-tag doubtful items and decide on them later. Set in order: give everything that is needed a set, marked place near where it is used, for example a board with tool outlines for hand tools, labelled racks for bar by size, and painted lines for the cylinder trolley. Shine: clean the area and the equipment, such as sweeping the booths and wiping down machines after isolating them, and look for faults like leaks or damaged cables while cleaning. Standardise: write down how the area should look and how it is cleaned, with checklists, photos and a roster, so everyone works the same way. Sustain: keep it up with training, regular audits and the team leader setting an example, so the area does not slip back to its old state.
markingPoints: Sort: remove what is not needed (red tags), with an example
Set in order: a marked place for each item, with an example
Shine: clean the area and equipment and look for faults, with an example
Standardise: written standard, checklist or roster, with an example
Sustain: training, audits and leading by example

essays.stem: Explain how you would set up waste segregation for a fabrication shop. Name the types of waste and say how each one should be handled.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would find out what waste the shop makes and the rules for each type, from the safety data sheets, the Centre's rules and the local authority. Then I would set up a waste station with clearly labelled bins. Clean steel offcuts, electrode stubs and swarf go into scrap metal bins and are sent to a scrap metal dealer for recycling. Paper, card and food waste go into general waste. Oily or solvent-soaked rags go in a closed metal bin with a self-closing lid, because they can catch fire. Used oil, solvents and paint waste are kept in closed, labelled containers and collected by an approved collector, never poured down a drain or onto the ground. Empty gas cylinders are marked EMPTY, kept apart and returned to the supplier. Batteries and fluorescent tubes are stored whole and sent for proper disposal. Cracked grinding discs are taken out of use. I would train the team, check the bins, and keep a record of each collection.
markingPoints: Finds out the waste types and rules (SDS, Centre's rules, local authority)
Labelled bins: scrap metal for recycling, general waste separate
Oily rags in a closed metal bin; oil, solvent and paint waste to an approved collector, never to drains
Empty cylinders marked and returned; batteries and tubes stored whole for proper disposal
Trains the team, checks the bins and keeps records

essays.stem: Describe how cleaning chemicals and solvents should be chosen, used, stored and disposed of in a fabrication workshop.
essays.modelAnswer: Before a chemical is used, read its label and safety data sheet (SDS) to learn its hazards, the PPE needed, how to store it and what to do in a spill or if it touches the skin or eyes. Choose the least harmful product that will do the job, such as a water-based degreaser instead of a strong solvent. Use it only in a well-ventilated area, away from welding, cutting and other sources of ignition, and wear the gloves and eye protection the SDS asks for. Dilute only as the maker says, and never mix different products, because some give off toxic gas. Never put chemicals in unmarked or drinks bottles; every container must be labelled. Store chemicals closed and labelled, with flammable ones in a fire-safe cabinet, away from oxygen cylinders and heat. Keep a spill kit near the store. Dispose of waste and empty containers as the SDS and the Centre's rules say, never down a drain, and wash your hands after use.
markingPoints: Reads the label and SDS first; chooses the least harmful product
Uses with ventilation, away from hot work, with the PPE the SDS gives
Dilutes as the maker says, never mixes products, never uses unlabelled containers
Stores closed and labelled; flammables in a fire-safe cabinet away from oxygen and heat; spill kit nearby
Disposes as the SDS and Centre's rules say, never down a drain

essays.stem: Explain how materials, tools and gas cylinders should be stored to keep a fabrication workshop safe and orderly, and say why.
essays.modelAnswer: Long bar and pipe should be stored flat on racks, sorted by size and grade and labelled, with the ends kept out of walkways; round items are chocked so they cannot roll. Sheet and plate go on racks within the rack's load rating, with the heaviest items low down, where they are safer to lift and less likely to fall. Hand tools go back to a board with tool outlines or a labelled drawer after use, so that missing or damaged tools are seen at once, and power tools are stored with their leads coiled. Consumables such as electrodes are kept dry, as the maker says. Gas cylinders are stored upright and chained, with valve caps on, in a ventilated, shaded place, with oxygen kept apart from fuel gas, and empty cylinders are marked and kept apart from full ones. Good storage keeps walkways and exits clear, stops falls, trips and fires, saves time spent looking for things and protects the stock from damage.
markingPoints: Bar and pipe flat on labelled racks, ends out of walkways, round items chocked
Sheet and plate within the rack rating, heavy items low
Tools returned to marked places; consumables kept dry as the maker says
Cylinders upright, chained, capped, ventilated, oxygen apart from fuel gas, empties marked
Gives reasons: clear walkways and exits, fewer falls, trips and fires, less time lost, stock protected

essays.stem: About 5 litres of hydraulic oil have leaked onto the workshop floor. Describe the steps you would take, from finding the spill to reporting it.
essays.modelAnswer: First warn people and keep them away, and put out wet floor signs or barriers. If it is safe, stop the leak at its source, for example by switching off and isolating the machine that is leaking, and put a drip tray under it. Check the SDS if the liquid is not known. Wear gloves and safety boots. Get the spill kit and put absorbent socks around the edge to stop the oil spreading, especially towards drains, then cover the spill with absorbent pads or granules. When the oil has soaked up, lift the used absorbent into a labelled bag or bin for hazardous waste, not the general bin. Clean the floor with a suitable degreaser so it is not slippery, and check that it is dry before removing the signs. Do not allow welding or cutting nearby until the area is clean. Report the spill and the leak, tag the machine out of use until it is repaired, and refill the spill kit.
markingPoints: Warns people and sets out signs or barriers
Stops the leak safely (isolates the machine, drip tray); checks the SDS; wears PPE
Contains with socks (away from drains), then absorbs with pads or granules
Used absorbent bagged as hazardous waste; floor degreased and dry; no hot work until clean
Reports the spill, tags the machine out of use and refills the spill kit

essays.stem: Explain how good housekeeping helps to prevent fires during welding and cutting, and describe what you would check before and after hot work.
essays.modelAnswer: Welding and cutting throw sparks and spatter a long way, and hot metal stays hot for a long time. Good housekeeping removes the fuel that a spark could light. Before hot work I would check that the area is clear of anything that can burn for at least 10 m, or as far as the hot work permit says: paper, card, rags, wood, oily waste and flammable liquids. Anything that cannot be moved is covered with fire blankets or screens. I would check for oil spills, and for cracks and gaps in the floor or walls where sparks could fall through. Gas hoses must be in good order and out of the spark path, an extinguisher must be close by, and the exits must be clear. A fire watch is kept during the work. After the work I would check the area again, including hidden places, and keep the fire watch for the time the permit or the Centre's rules give, often 30 to 60 minutes, then sign off. Stubs and hot offcuts go into metal containers.
markingPoints: Explains that housekeeping removes fuel for sparks and spatter
Before: combustibles cleared or covered for at least 10 m or as the permit says; spills cleaned; gaps checked
Before: hoses in good order and out of the spark path; extinguisher at hand; exits clear
Fire watch during the work
After: area rechecked, fire watch kept for the set time, signed off; hot stubs in metal containers

essays.stem: Describe how you would carry out a housekeeping inspection of the workshop, record the results and make sure the faults are fixed.
essays.modelAnswer: I would use a written checklist that covers each area: walkways and exits, floors and spills, benches and booths, storage racks, gas cylinders, cables and leads, tools, chemicals, waste bins, fire extinguishers, lighting and extraction. I would agree the time with the supervisor and walk round the whole workshop, looking closely and taking photos of any problems. For each item I record whether it is satisfactory, and for each fault I write what it is, where it is and how serious it is. Anything dangerous, such as a damaged lead, is dealt with at once: it is taken out of use and tagged. For the other faults I agree an action, give each one an owner and a date, and write it on an action list. I work out the score, for example as a percentage, so it can be compared with the last inspection. I sign and date the checklist, give a copy to the supervisor, and check later that each action has been done.
markingPoints: Uses a checklist that covers all areas of the workshop
Walks the whole area, records each item and describes each fault with its place and seriousness (photos)
Deals with dangerous faults at once (out of use and tagged)
Action list with an owner and a date for each fault; score worked out
Signs, dates and passes on the record, and checks that actions are done

essays.stem: A new trainee in your team does not see why housekeeping matters. Explain how you would coach him and check that he keeps to the standard.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would talk with the trainee in private and explain why housekeeping matters, using real examples: cables and offcuts cause trips, oily rags and paper catch fire from sparks, lost tools waste time, and a tidy bay shows customers good work. I would show him the standard: what a clean bay looks like, where each tool goes and which waste goes in which bin, and I would work alongside him the first time. I would agree clear tasks with him, written on the roster, and make sure he has the brooms, bins and PPE he needs. I would check his area at the end of each shift and give quick, fair feedback, praising what is done well and pointing out what is missed. If he still does not keep to the standard, I would talk with him again, record it and, if needed, refer it to the supervisor. I would also set the example myself, because a team copies its leader.
markingPoints: Talks privately and explains the reasons with real examples (trips, fire, lost time, image)
Shows the standard and works alongside him at first
Agrees clear tasks on the roster and makes sure the equipment and PPE are there
Checks regularly and gives fair feedback, praising good work
Follows up, records and refers if needed; leads by example

essays.stem: Describe how to clean welding and cutting equipment and workshop machines safely at the end of a shift, including the fume extraction, and say what you would report.
essays.modelAnswer: First switch off the machines and isolate them at the supply, and close the gas cylinder valves and bleed the hoses as the maker's instructions say. Let hot equipment and work cool, and mark hot items. Wear gloves and eye protection. Remove slag, stubs and offcuts from the booth, put stubs in a metal container, and brush down the bench. Clean grinding dust with a vacuum or a damp cloth, not compressed air. Clear swarf from saws and drills with a brush or swarf hook once they have stopped, never by hand. Coil cables and hoses and hang them up, checking them for damage as you do so. Empty the extractor's spark trap and check its filters; clean or change them only as the maker's manual says, with the unit switched off. Put tools back in their places. Any fault found, such as a damaged lead, a leaking hose or a blocked filter, is tagged out of use and reported to the supervisor, and the check is recorded.
markingPoints: Switches off and isolates machines; closes cylinders and bleeds hoses as the maker says
Lets things cool; wears PPE; stubs and slag cleared into metal containers
Safe cleaning: vacuum or damp wipe, swarf hook or brush on stopped machines, never by hand or compressed air
Cables and hoses coiled and checked; extractor spark trap and filters dealt with as the maker says
Faults tagged out of use, reported and recorded

practical1.title: Plan and carry out a 5S improvement of a fabrication bay
practical1.brief: The assessor names one fabrication bay at the Centre (for example a welding booth, its bench and the storage beside it). As a team, plan and carry out a 5S improvement of the bay. First take 'before' photos and score the bay with the Centre's housekeeping checklist. Then write a short plan: the tasks, who leads each of the five steps, the PPE and the time for each step. Carry out the five steps: Sort (red-tag items that are not needed and agree what happens to them), Set in order (give each tool and item a marked place, for example tool outlines on a board and labels on shelves), Shine (clean the bay, the bench and the equipment, with the equipment switched off and isolated), Standardise (write a one-page standard and a cleaning roster for the bay) and Sustain (score the bay again and agree how it will be kept up). Each member leads at least one step and takes part in all of them. Photograph each stage below and add the photos, the plan, both scores and the standard to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: The Centre's housekeeping checklist (two copies: before and after)
Red tags, markers and a marked holding area for tagged items
Labels, floor marking tape, and a board with paint or marker for tool outlines
Brooms, dustpans, a vacuum with a suitable filter, cloths and bins
Cleaning products with their safety data sheets
Gloves, safety glasses and dust masks for each member
Plan sheet, roster sheet and pens
photos: The bay before the work, from a fixed spot, with the 'before' score
The written plan showing who leads each step
Red-tagged items in the holding area
Tools and items in their new marked places
A member cleaning equipment that is switched off and isolated
The bay after the work, from the same spot
The standard and roster posted in the bay, with the 'after' score
checklist: Took part in scoring the bay and writing the plan
Led their step clearly and helped with the other steps
Wore the right PPE and isolated equipment before cleaning it
Used safe cleaning methods (vacuum or damp wipe, no compressed air on dust)
Sorted waste into the right bins
Gave items a clear, marked place that others can follow
Helped write a standard and roster that are clear and workable
Scored the bay again and explained the improvement and how it will be kept up
safety: Switch off and isolate any machine or welding set before cleaning it
Do not use compressed air to clear dust; use a vacuum or a damp cloth
Read the SDS and wear the PPE it asks for when using cleaning products
Lift heavy items with a team lift or a trolley
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Workshop housekeeping inspection, spill drill and waste station
practical2.brief: As a team, inspect the Centre's fabrication workshop, deal with a practice spill and set up a waste segregation station. (1) Split the workshop into areas. Each member inspects one area with the housekeeping checklist, records each fault with a photo, says how serious it is, fixes simple faults safely, and tags and lists anything that needs a repair. (2) The assessor sets out a practice spill of water with a little food colouring. One member leads the response and the others take set roles: warn people and set out signs, contain the spill with socks, absorb it, bag the waste, clean and dry the floor, and report. (3) Set up a waste station with labelled bins for scrap metal, general waste, oily rags (a closed metal bin) and hazardous waste, and a sign that shows what goes where. (4) Write a short inspection report with an action list that gives each fault an owner and a date. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and the report to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.

checklist: Inspected their area fully and recorded faults accurately

safety: Do not touch electrical faults: tag the item and report it

Wear gloves when handling waste and used absorbent
Lift full bins with care, or use a trolley
